UNPAID TRIAL WORK / WORKING INTERVIEW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California wage-and-hour law as it applies to time Jordan T. Reyes spends performing an actual work trial, skills demonstration, working interview, or unpaid trial shift in connection with Acme, Inc.'s hiring process for the Line Cook position -- as distinct from ordinary interview conversation, watching a demonstration, completing a written test, or touring a workplace. It summarizes selected provisions of the California Labor Code and the applicable Industrial Welfare Commission wage order addressing when time is compensable "hours worked" regardless of whether the person performing it has been formally hired. It is not a determination that any specific activity Jordan T. Reyes performed, or will perform, for Acme, Inc. during the hiring process is or is not compensable work, and it does not itself calculate any amount owed.

WHO COUNTS AS "EMPLOYED": THE WAGE ORDER'S DEFINITIONS
Under the wage order that governs professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations, "employ" is defined broadly, and "employee" is defined in terms of that broad definition. Neither definition turns on whether a hiring decision has been made, whether the person has signed an offer letter, or what label -- "applicant," "candidate," "trainee," or "trial worker" -- the business uses for the person performing the activity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Employ” means to engage, suffer, or permit to work."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(F), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(F) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "“Employee” means any person employed by an employer."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(G), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(G) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is Wage Order 4-2001's own numbering (the order covering professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations); California's other numbered wage orders (for example, Wage Order 5 for the public housekeeping industry or Wage Order 7 for the mercantile industry) contain their own definitions section, and while their "employ"/"employee" language is understood to be substantially similar across the numbered wage orders, this document verified Wage Order 4-2001's text only -- it does not independently confirm the wording or numbering in the other sixteen wage orders, and which order applies to a given business depends on its industry or the occupation involved. This clause also does not by itself resolve whether a specific pre-hire activity was actually "work" within these definitions -- it establishes only that the wage order recognizes no separate, lesser category of coverage for someone who has not yet formally been offered or accepted a job.

NO STATUTORY EXCEPTION FOR TRIAL, TRYOUT, OR INTERVIEW WORK
California's minimum wage statute ties the duty to pay to whether the wage fixed by the applicable wage order or other law was paid to a covered worker -- it does not carve out an exception based on the label attached to the activity, such as a job interview, tryout, working interview, orientation, or unpaid trial period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The minimum wage for employees fixed by the commission or by any applicable state or local law, is the minimum wage to be paid to employees, and the payment of a lower wage than the minimum so fixed is unlawful."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 1197 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.)
  Known gap: Section 1197 sets the floor at whatever minimum wage is "fixed by the commission or by any applicable state or local law" -- it does not itself state a dollar figure, and it does not itself define who counts as an "employee" to whom it applies (that question is addressed by the wage order definitions cited elsewhere in this document, not by this section). Dozens of California cities and counties have adopted local minimum wage ordinances setting a floor higher than the statewide rate; this document does not catalog local ordinances, and the rate actually owed for a specific trial-work arrangement depends on the work location.

AN AGREEMENT TO WORK UNPAID DOES NOT OVERRIDE THIS DUTY
California law gives a worker who was paid less than the applicable minimum wage a civil right to recover the shortfall, and it says this right exists notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage -- meaning a person's own advance agreement to perform trial work, a tryout, or a working interview without pay does not, by itself, extinguish a claim for the unpaid minimum wage if the activity performed was covered work.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage, any employee receiving less than the legal minimum wage or the legal overtime compensation applicable to the employee is entitled to recover in a civil action the unpaid balance of the full amount of this minimum wage or overtime compensation, including interest thereon, reasonable attorney’s fees, and costs of suit."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1194(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 1194, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1194.)
  Known gap: Section 1194 refers throughout to "employee" without itself defining that term -- whether a specific person performing trial or tryout work was legally an "employee" at all, as opposed to a genuine unpaid observer who performed no work, is a threshold, fact-specific question this document does not resolve; see the wage order definitions cited elsewhere in this document for the applicable standard. This document also does not verify whether any published California appellate decision has applied Section 1194 specifically to a pre-hire trial-work or working-interview scenario: an attempted CourtListener case-law search for on-point authority (query: unpaid trial work period "working interview" minimum wage California, California courts) returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, "Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") rather than results, and this document does not substitute case law recalled from memory for a verified search.

THE CURRENT STATEWIDE MINIMUM WAGE RATE
Absent a higher state or local minimum wage or another applicable exception, the statewide minimum wage under the wage order that governs professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations is currently $16.90 per hour for all hours worked.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Sixteen dollars and ninety cents ($16.90) per hour for all hours worked, effective January 1, 2026"
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(A)(1), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 4(A)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is the wage order's own default statewide figure, not necessarily the rate that applies everywhere in California. Numerous California cities and counties (among them Los Angeles, San Francisco, and dozens of others) have adopted local minimum wage ordinances that set a floor higher than this statewide figure, and separate, sector-specific minimum wage schedules apply to some occupations (for example, certain fast food and health care employees) under other statutes this document does not verify or cite. This clause verified only the Wage Order 4-2001 text current as of the September 2026 fetch date and reflects the rate effective January 1, 2026; it will become outdated once the Department of Industrial Relations publishes a new adjusted rate for a later year.

NO SMALL-EMPLOYER OR FIRST-HIRE EXCEPTION
The wage order's minimum wage duty applies to every covered employer regardless of size -- including a business making its first hire and running a trial shift before that hire is finalized. Nothing in the wage order's minimum wage section conditions the duty on the employer having a minimum number of employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in Subdivision (E) of this section, every employer, regardless of the number of employees, shall pay to each employee wages not less than the following:"
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(A), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 4(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This clause's quote runs across a line break in the source PDF ("pay to" / "each employee"); the fetched PDF text was joined with a single space at that line break rather than quoted with the mid-word line-wrap left in, a normalization confirmed against the raw extracted PDF text and not a substantive change. The wage order text quoted here begins "Except as provided in Subdivision (E)," which is a separate minimum wage schedule for certain covered health care facilities that this document does not describe. This section also contains a "Learners" provision, in the same subdivision, permitting an employer to pay as little as 85 percent of the minimum wage, rounded to the nearest nickel, during an employee's first 160 hours of employment in an occupation in which the employee has no previous similar or related experience -- a provision that could apply to some trial-work arrangements and that this document does not otherwise analyze or apply.

PAYROLL RECORD DUTY ONCE TRIAL WORK IS PAID
If Acme, Inc. pays Jordan T. Reyes for time worked during a trial or working-interview period, California law imposes the same payroll recordkeeping duty on that pay as on any other wage payment: an employer must keep payroll records showing the hours worked and the wages paid.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Keep, at a central location in the state or at the plants or establishments at which employees are employed, payroll records showing the hours worked daily by and the wages paid to, and the number of piece-rate units earned by and any applicable piece rate paid to, employees employed at the respective plants or establishments."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1174(d) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 1174, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1174.)
  Known gap: Section 1174(d) also requires these records be kept "on file for not less than three years," a retention duration this clause's quoted text does not restate but that appears in the same subdivision. This document does not address the separate itemized wage-statement duty under Labor Code Section 226 or the waiting-time penalty for a willful failure to pay wages due at separation under Section 203, both of which are addressed by other documents already in this corpus and are not duplicated here. This clause also assumes the trial work was actually paid -- it does not itself say what recordkeeping or other obligation, if any, attaches when trial work should have been paid under the standard described elsewhere in this document but was not.

RECORD OF THE TRIAL WORK ARRANGEMENT
Company: Acme, Inc.
Applicant: Jordan T. Reyes
Position applied for: Line Cook
Date(s) of the trial work period: September 15, 2026

Nature of the activity: ☐ Applicant performed actual production or service work (for example: preparing food, cutting a customer's hair, driving a delivery route, operating equipment, or working a live shift on the floor)  ☐ Applicant observed, was interviewed, completed a written or skills test, or toured the workplace without performing production or service work  ☐ Other (describe): _______________________________________________

Was Jordan T. Reyes paid for this time? ☐ Yes, at $16.90 per hour or more  ☐ No  ☐ Other arrangement (describe): _______________________________________________

Who benefited from any work performed: ☐ Acme, Inc. received the output of the work performed (for example: food served to a paying customer, a haircut given to a paying client, or a delivery completed for a paying customer)  ☐ No output of Jordan T. Reyes's activity was used or sold by Acme, Inc.  ☐ Other (describe): _______________________________________________

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan T. Reyes and Acme, Inc. each acknowledge that they have reviewed the record above and this information sheet's description of the California wage-and-hour standards that can apply to trial work performed during a hiring process.

Executed on September 15, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan T. Reyes: ☐ _________________________

Signature on behalf of Acme, Inc.: ☐ _________________________
